author: Skaidrīte Saduka un Ligita Liepiņa
title_lv: Caur sniegu un asarām līdz piena galdam
title_en: Through snow and tears to the milk churn stand
text_lv:
Skaidrīte raksta.
Man ir pilni 73 gadi vēl gotiņas slaucu un nesu pienu uz piena galda ar kannām.

Gandrīz visu savu mūžu izņemot kādus dažus gadus no sava mūža, kad dzīvoju Ogrē.
Sāku gotiņas slaukt no 5 gadiņiem, 10 gadu vecumā kā meitenīte mācēju, jau visus darbus. Man gotiņas ir mīļas, kā ģimenes locekļi.

Nu jau piena galds ir vecs sāk apsūnot, kā arī mēs paliekam veci nevis jaunāki, bet dzīvojam, dzīve neapstājas, bet griežas dzīves ritenis uz priekšu.

No jaunības gadiem cieši atmiņā ir palicis: Bija tādi sniega kalni, ka zirgs vilka ragavas līdz vēderam laukā uz lielā ceļa līdz piena galdam.
Citreiz ar ragaviņām 4 km raudādama vilku uz lielā ceļa a kur vēl slidenais ceļš ka asaras un puņķi bija. Vēl jau kannas bija jādabū uz piena galda, cik tas prasīja spēka.

Vēl bija grūti, kad lielāku laiku ziemā bija auksts mīnus 20 līdz mīnus 30 grādu grūti bija tas, ka pienam nedrīkstēja sasalušam. Bet viss ir izdzīvots.

Agrāk slaucu ar rokām no 3 līdz 5 gotiņām. Viss ir piedzīvots un izdzīvots, grūti bijis, bet, kad saulīte lec, bet Tu jau esi uz rindas vai aukstā rasa un lietainie rīti, tas viss dod spēku strādāt uz priekšu.

Siens arī bija jāsagatavo, kasām lielāku daļu ar grābekļiem, bet tagad jau vieglāk - atbrauc traktors un darbiņš padarīts.
text_en:
Skaidrīte writes.
I am a full 73 years old, and I still milk cows and carry the milk in cans to the milk churn stand. I've done this for almost my entire life, except for a few years when I lived in Ogre.

I started milking cows when I was 5 years old, and by the age of 10, as a little girl, I already knew how to do all the farm chores. The cows are dear to me, like members of the family.

By now, the milk churn stand is old and starting to gather moss, just as we are getting older instead of younger. But we keep living; life doesn't stop, the wheel of life keeps turning forward.

A vivid memory from my youth: the snowbanks were so high that the horse would be belly-deep in the snow while pulling the sled out to the main road, to the milk churn stand. Other times, I would pull the sled for 4 kilometers to the main road myself, crying—especially on the slippery roads, full of tears and a runny nose. And after all that, the cans still had to be lifted onto the milk churn stand, which took so much strength.

It was also hard during long winter stretches when it was minus 20 to minus 30 degrees cold. The hardest part was making sure the milk didn't freeze. But we survived it all.

In the past, I used to hand-milk 3 to 5 cows. I have experienced and lived through it all. It has been hard, but when the sun rises and you're already out working in the rows, or during the cold dew and rainy mornings, it all gives you the strength to keep going.

We also had to prepare the hay, raking most of it by hand, but it's much easier now—a tractor arrives and the job is done.

author: Renāte Zīdere
title_en: Let's meet at the milk churn stand!
text_lv:
Kaut pats piena steķītis savas dienas vada kādā malkas šķūnītī, bet par godu ilgu gadu kalpošanai Dikļu miestiņa centrā dzīvojošajiem govju turētājiem, nu ieguvis tīri vai vietvārda cienīgu nosaukumu.

Pats miestiņš saglabājis tā vēsturiskā nosaukuma noskaņu. To palīdz uzturēt simtgadīgo ozolu aleja, kuras zaļā lapotne abpus ceļa malai vasarās gājējus un braucējus ved kā caur zaļam tunelim, kura sākums ir Muiža un noslēgums Baznīca. Vien dažas sociālisma laika ēkas alejas malā liecina par laikmetu griežiem Dikļos. Viena no tādām ir daudzdzīvokļu māja “Lazdas”, kura uzcelta pārsimts metrus no alejas pašā Dikļu parka malā. Kā jau tā laika lauku apbūves noteikumi paredzēja - ja ir māja, tad jābūt arī kūtiņām. Tās tika būvētas otrpus alejai. Gandrīz visiem “Lazdu” mājas iedzīvotājiem bija kāds kūtiņā turams lopiņš, arī gotiņa, kuras pārstrādātajam nodotais piens papildināja ģimenes budžetu. Lai piena kannas un kanniņas nebūtu jāliek ceļmalas smiltī, kā visur citur Latvijas laukos, arī “Lazdu” mājas govju saimniekiem tika tapināts pieklājīgs piena steķis.

Tolaik “Lazdās” dzīvoja kolhoza speciālisti, pedagogi, kāds mediķis un milicis, vārdu sakot - ciema inteliģence, kura starp visiem tiešajiem un ģimenes saimnieciskajiem darbiem prata izbrīvēt laiku arī tuvākiem un tālākiem kultūras pasākumus. Ja braucēju bija vairāk, tika algots kopīgs autobuss, kura maršrutā bija dikliešu noteiktas pieturvietas. Piemēram - Baznīca alejas tālākajā galā un Sarkanais laukums pie veikala centrā, bet pa vidu, pretī “Lazdām” - Piena steķis. Vēlāk šoferīši šos nosaukumus ielāgoja un bez gariem paskaidrojumiem pieturas ievēroja.

Tagad, kad steķītis sen savu kalpošanu beidzis, tā iezīmētā vieta turpina dzīvot un atgādināt par laikiem, kad saule bija spožāka, debesis zilākas un paša slauktais pieniņš trekns, balts un smaržīgs.

Mazs atmiņu atplaiksnījums par piena steķīti Dikļos.
Ar domām, atmiņām un sirdsmīlestību Dikļos, Renāte Zīdere.
text_en:
Although the little milk churn stand itself now spends its days in a woodshed, in honor of its many years of service to the cow keepers living in the center of the village of Dikļi, it has earned a title truly worthy of a place name.

The village itself has preserved the atmosphere of its historic name. This is sustained by the avenue of century-old oaks; in the summer, its green foliage on both sides of the road guides pedestrians and drivers as if through a verdant tunnel, beginning at the Manor and ending at the Church. Only a few Soviet-era buildings along the avenue stand as testaments to the changing times in Dikļi. One such building is the apartment house “Lazdas” (Hazels), built a couple of hundred meters from the avenue, right on the edge of the Dikļi park. As the rural building regulations of that era dictated - if there is a house, there must also be sheds for livestock. These were built on the other side of the avenue. Almost all the residents of the “Lazdas” house kept some animal in their shed, including cows, whose milk, when handed over for processing, supplemented the family budget. To avoid having to set the large and small milk cans down in the roadside sand, as was common everywhere else in the Latvian countryside, a proper milk churn stand was built for the cow owners of the “Lazdas” house.

At the time, “Lazdas” was home to collective farm specialists, teachers, a medic, and a policeman - in short, the village intelligentsia. Amidst all their primary jobs and household chores, they still managed to carve out time for cultural events, both near and far. When there was a larger group of travelers, a shared bus would be hired, following a route with stops designated by the locals. For example - the Church at the far end of the avenue, and the Red Square by the shop in the center, but right in the middle, opposite “Lazdas” - the Milk Churn Stand. Over time, the bus drivers learned these names by heart and would observe the stops without needing lengthy explanations.

Today, long after the little milk churn stand has finished its service, the spot it marked lives on, serving as a reminder of a time when the sun was brighter, the sky was bluer, and the milk drawn by one's own hands was rich, white, and fragrant.

A brief glimpse of memories about the milk churn stand in Dikļi.
With thoughts, memories, and heartfelt love in Dikļi, Renāte Zīdere.
